etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Early Modern English laune (“turf, grassy area”), alteration of laund (“glade”), from Middle English launde, from Old French lande (“heath, moor”), of Germanic or Gaulish origin, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”) or Proto-Celtic *landā, both from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).

Akin to Breton lann (“heath”), Old Norse & Old English land. Doublet of land and lande.

definitions.definition: Ground (generally in front of or around a house) covered with grass kept closely mown.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path […]. It twisted and turned, […] and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn. And, back of the lawn, was a big, old-fashioned house, with piazzas stretching in front of it, and all blazing with lights. 'Twas the house I'd seen the roof of from the beach.

definitions.definition: (England, historical or regional) An open space between woods.
(biology) An overgrown agar culture, such that no separation between single colonies exists.

quote.citation: 1827, An Historical, Antiquarian, and Picturesque Account of Kirkstall Abbey, page 170:
quote.text: By opening all the arches of the several apartments  […] , by lawning the area within, and by a judicious use of ivy where any blank spaces require to be broken, or any deformities concealed, this might be made a beautiful and singular scene;  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Apparently from Laon, a French town known for its linen manufacturing, from Old French Lan, from Latin Laudunum, a Celtic name cognate with Lugdunum.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A type of thin linen or cotton.

quote.citation: 1726 October 28, [Jonathan Swift], “Of the Inhabitants of Lilliput; […]”, in Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.  […]  [Gulliver’s Travels], volume I, London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, part I (A Voyage to Lilliput), pages 107–108:
quote.text: Two hundred Sempſtreſſes were employed to make me Shirts, and Linen for Bed and Table, all of the ſtrongeft and coarſeſt kind they could get; which, however, they were forced to quilt together in ſeveral Folds, for the thickeſt was ſome degrees finer than Lawn.

quote.citation: 1897, Bram Stoker, Dracula, New York, N.Y.: Modern Library, →OCLC:
quote.text: The stream had trickled over her chin and stained the purity of her lawn death robe.

quote.citation: 1939, Raymond Chandler, The Big Sleep, Penguin, published 2011, page 144:
quote.text: He looked through the glass at the fire, set it down on the end of the desk and wiped his lips with a sheer lawn handkerchief.

definitions.definition: (in the plural) Pieces of this fabric, especially as used for the sleeves of a bishop.
(countable, obsolete) A piece of clothing made from lawn.

quote.citation: 1910, Margaret Hill McCarter, The Price of the Prairie:
quote.text: […]  she was as the wild yoncopin to the calla lily. Marjie knew how to dress. To-day, shaded by the buggy-top, in her dainty light blue lawn, with the soft pink of her cheeks and her clear white brow and throat, she was a most delicious thing  […]
